chapter_title: Concurrency with Grand Central Dispatch and Async/Await

screens.title: Concurrency with Grand Central Dispatch and Async/Await
screens.subtitle: Keep the UI responsive by moving heavy work off the main thread and adopting Swift's structured concurrency

narration.text: In this lesson you will understand why concurrency matters for any iOS app that needs to stay responsive while doing work in the background. We start from a simple user-experience problem: long tasks on the main thread freeze the interface. Then you will learn two practical toolsets. First, Grand Central Dispatch, a queue-based system that safely schedules work on the main queue or on background global queues using quality-of-service hints. You will see the common pattern of performing heavy work on a background queue and then switching to the main queue to update the UI. Second, you will explore Swift's modern concurrency features: async functions, await, Task, Task. detached, and the MainActor. These features give you structured, readable asynchronous code and help avoid many mistakes caused by nested callbacks. We will also highlight common pitfalls like race conditions, deadlocks, and retain cycles, and show simple ways to mitigate them. By the end you will know when to use GCD and when async/await makes your code safer and clearer.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Concurrency keeps the UI responsive by moving long tasks off the main thread; use GCD for explicit queue control and async/await for structured, readable async code.

screens.title: What is concurrency and why it matters
screens.subtitle: Definition, real impact on UI responsiveness, and a concrete example

narration.text: Concurrency is the ability of an application to make progress on more than one task by interleaving their execution or running them on separate threads. In practice, this means your app can fetch data, process images, or perform calculations while still responding to touches, animations, and user input. The main practical consequence for iOS is that the main thread handles all UI updates and input; if you perform a long-running synchronous task there, the interface will freeze. A concrete example is computing a large sum or processing many images in a loop on the main thread — while that work runs, buttons do not respond and animations stutter. A common misconception is that starting a function from view lifecycle automatically runs it off the main thread; in truth most lifecycle closures run on the main thread unless you explicitly offload work. To avoid this, move heavy operations to background queues or async tasks, and bring results back to the main thread for UI updates. Think of concurrency as separating concerns: computation and input and output happen in the background, presentation stays on the main actor. A practical question to keep in mind is: if a task can take more than a few hundred milliseconds, should it run off the main thread? Usually the answer is yes.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Concurrency prevents UI blocking by running heavy work separately from the main thread; always keep main for UI tasks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › What is concurrency?
Short definition

Concurrency is interleaving or parallel execution of tasks so an app can remain responsive while work continues in the background.

Concrete example
Imagine filtering 200 images. Doing this on the main thread will freeze scrolling. Move filtering to a background queue and update visible images on the main thread.
Misconception
Starting work in onAppear does not move it off the main thread automatically. You must use a Task or a dispatch queue.
Visual mnemonic
Main Thread
UI events • animations • view updates
Background
Network • computation • file I/O
Key Takeaway

If a task can take noticeable time, run it off the main thread and then dispatch results back to the main thread for UI updates.

screens.title: Grand Central Dispatch basics
screens.subtitle: Main queue, global queues, and QoS levels

narration.text: Grand Central Dispatch is Apple's queue-based C A P I for scheduling work. At its core are dispatch queues: serial or concurrent queues that execute closures. The main queue is a serial queue tied to the main thread and must be used for any UI updates. Global queues are concurrent and provided with different quality-of-service levels such as userInitiated, utility, and background. Use userInitiated for work the user is waiting for, utility for longer background tasks like file input and output, and background for maintenance tasks with low priority. The typical pattern is: start a heavy task on a global queue, perform work there, and then dispatch UI updates to DispatchQueue. main. async. A common mistake is updating UI directly from a background queue or performing expensive work on the main queue; both lead to bugs or UI jank. As an example, use DispatchQueue. global(qos:. userInitiated). async to compute a result and then DispatchQueue. main. async to assign that result to a published property or update a view. Remember to consider QoS when multiple tasks compete for C P U time — it guides system scheduling. What will you prioritize in your app: immediate user feedback or low-priority background maintenance?

keyIdea.title: GCD pattern
keyIdea.text: Use global queues with appropriate QoS for background work and always update UI on DispatchQueue.main.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › GCD Basics
Queues
Main Queue — serial, UI updates only. Access with DispatchQueue.main.
Global Queues — concurrent, use DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated) or other QoS levels.
QoS — choose priority that matches the user's expectation for that work.
Process
1. Dispatch background task
2. Do work
3. Dispatch to main for UI
When to prefer which QoS
  • .userInitiated — user waits for result, update UI quickly.
  • .utility — longer tasks that benefit the user but are not instantaneous.
  • .background — low-priority maintenance like syncing or prefetching.
Example code
// GCD pattern
DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated).async {
  // perform heavy work
  let result = performWork()
  DispatchQueue.main.async {
    // update UI with result
    updateViews(result)
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Pick an appropriate QoS for background tasks and always perform UI work on the main queue.

screens.title: GCD example: heavy calculation
screens.subtitle: Step through a concrete DispatchQueue example and UI update

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical GCD example that simulates a heavy calculation. The pattern uses a global queue to run the long loop and then DispatchQueue. main. async to update the UI. In the example we print start and finish messages and compute a large sum inside the background closure. The important teaching points are: first, the heavy loop runs on a background queue so the main thread remains responsive; second, any UI-related assignment must be dispatched back to the main queue. A common misconception is that print statements inside a background closure run on the main thread; they run on whatever queue you dispatched to. Also be careful about capturing self in closures; if you update properties on self that affect UI, use weak captures or ensure the owner is on the main actor. In UIKit or SwiftUI, updating a label or a @Published value should happen on the main thread. Try to spot where you might add [weak self] in a real app and consider marking the view model with MainActor instead to simplify safety. Reflect: when you see nested closures, ask whether structured concurrency could make this code easier to read.

keyIdea.title: GCD example takeaway
keyIdea.text: Run heavy loops on a global queue and always dispatch UI updates to the main queue; mind captures to avoid retain cycles.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › GCD Example
Annotated code
// GCD Example
func performHeavyCalculation() {
    print("Starting heavy calculation on background thread...")
    DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated).async {
        // Simulate a long-running task
        var sum = 0
        for i in 0..<1_000_000_000 {
            sum += i
        }
        let result = "Calculation complete: \(sum)"
        print("Calculation finished on background thread.")

        // Update UI on the main thread
        DispatchQueue.main.async {
            // Update a SwiftUI Text view or UIKit label here
            print("UI updated with result: \(result)")
        }
    }
}
Note: heavy work runs inside DispatchQueue.global(...).async; the final UI update is wrapped in DispatchQueue.main.async to ensure UI-safety.
Remember to avoid capturing strong references to owners inside long-lived closures. Use weak self or MainActor patterns for view models.
Check your understanding
  • Why must UI updates happen on the main thread?
  • Where would you add a weak self capture in this code?
  • Could async/await make this code simpler? When?
Common mistake

Updating UI from inside the background closure without switching to DispatchQueue.main will cause unpredictable behavior; always marshal UI changes to main.

screens.title: Swift's async/await and structured concurrency
screens.subtitle: What async functions, await, Task, and MainActor mean

narration.text: Swift introduced async/await to make asynchronous code read more like synchronous code and to provide structured concurrency. An async function is declared with the async keyword and indicates it can suspend while waiting for work. When you call an async function you use await — this pauses the current task until the result is ready, while letting the runtime run other tasks. Task is the unit of work in this model; you can create a Task to execute async code from synchronous contexts, and Task. detached for unstructured lifetimes that are not tied to a parent. The MainActor is a global actor that guarantees code annotated with @MainActor runs on the main thread, so marking a view model with @MainActor simplifies UI updates and avoids explicit dispatching. A concrete example is a DataFetcher with a fetchData async method: mark the class @MainActor, set isLoading true, await a network call, then update data and isLoading. Misconception check: await does not create a new thread by itself; it suspends the current task and yields to the scheduler. The closing question: how would you decide between DispatchQueue and async/await for a particular task?

keyIdea.title: Async/await insight
keyIdea.text: Async/await suspends tasks instead of nesting callbacks, and MainActor ensures UI updates run on the main thread.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Async/Await
Key terms
async — marks a function that can suspend.
await — pauses until an async call completes without blocking the thread.
Task — unit of async work; use Task { await ... } to call async from sync code.
MainActor — annotates code to always run on the main thread.
Example snippet
@MainActor
class DataFetcher: ObservableObject {
    @Published var data: String = "No data"
    @Published var isLoading: Bool = false

    func fetchData() async {
        isLoading = true
        try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 2 * 1_000_000_000)
        data = "Data fetched successfully!"
        isLoading = false
    }
}
This pattern keeps UI state on the main actor and avoids explicit DispatchQueue.main.async calls when updating published properties.

screens.title: Async/await example: Image loader activity
screens.subtitle: Using TaskGroup to perform concurrent downloads and publish on MainActor

narration.text: This hands-on activity shows a common modern pattern: concurrently download images with async/await and update the UI safely. The ImageLoader class is annotated with MainActor so its @Published properties are updated on the main thread automatically. Inside loadImages you can use a throwing TaskGroup to create multiple concurrent download tasks or use async let for a simpler approach. Each download awaits URLSession. shared. data(from:), converts the data to an image, and appends it to the published array. Important details: wrap network calls with try await to propagate errors, clear previous state before beginning, and set isLoading true at the start and false at the end. Misconceptions: TaskGroup does not guarantee ordering of results; append results as they arrive if order is not required, or collect them in a consistent index if order matters. Also, because ImageLoader is MainActor, you don't need to dispatch back to the main queue after each download. Try modifying the code to use async let and compare readability and cancellation behavior. Closing thought: structured concurrency helps you reason about lifetime and cancellation of related tasks. Async/await example: Image loader activity means use taskgroup or async let to download concurrently and let mainactor handle safe ui updates for published state.. In practical terms, using taskgroup to perform concurrent downloads and publish on mainactor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: TaskGroup pattern
keyIdea.text: Use TaskGroup or async let to download concurrently and let MainActor handle safe UI updates for published state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Image Loader
Starter code overview
@MainActor
class ImageLoader: ObservableObject {
    @Published var loadedImages: [UIImage] = []
    @Published var isLoading: Bool = false
    @Published var errorMessage: String?

    func loadImages(from urls: [URL]) async {
        isLoading = true
        errorMessage = nil
        loadedImages = []

        await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: UIImage?.self) { group in
            for url in urls {
                group.addTask {
                    do {
                        let (data, _) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url)
                        return UIImage(data: data)
                    } catch {
                        return nil
                    }
                }
            }

            for await image in group {
                if let image = image {
                    self.loadedImages.append(image)
                }
            }
        }

        isLoading = false
    }
}
Note: because the class is @MainActor, appending images updates the published property safely on the main thread. If you removed MainActor, you would need explicit dispatching.
Also consider cancellation: wrap long downloads with checks for Task.isCancelled and use URLSession tasks that support cancellation.
Practical tips
  • Use TaskGroup to control concurrency and collect results.
  • Use async let for simpler concurrent awaits when ordering is predictable.
  • Mark view models with @MainActor to avoid explicit main dispatching for UI state.
Key Takeaway

Structured concurrency lets you fetch many items concurrently and update UI state safely when using MainActor.

screens.title: GCD vs async/await
screens.subtitle: When to use explicit queues and when to choose structured concurrency

narration.text: Both GCD and async/await let you perform work off the main thread, but they serve slightly different developer needs. GCD gives you low-level control over specific queues and quality of service. It's useful when you need explicit control, custom serial queues, or when integrating with legacy C APIs. Async/await offers structured concurrency: async functions, Tasks, TaskGroup, and actors that express relationships between tasks and make cancellation and error propagation easier. A concrete contrast: for a one-off background computation you might use DispatchQueue. global(). async; for a set of related asynchronous operations that should cancel together or return structured results, async/await with a TaskGroup is clearer. Misconception: async/await always replaces GCD — not necessarily. Under the hood Swift still uses system scheduling; use GCD for fine-grained queue policies or when you already manage queues. When migrating, prefer async/await for readability and safer cancellation, but keep GCD for interoperability or performance tuning when needed. Which pattern will make your code easier to test and reason about? GCD vs async/await means use gcd for explicit queue control and async/await for structured, readable concurrency and easier cancellation.. In practical terms, when to use explicit queues and when to choose structured concurrency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose by need
keyIdea.text: Use GCD for explicit queue control and async/await for structured, readable concurrency and easier cancellation.

Grand Central Dispatch
Low-level queue control, serial or concurrent queues, QoS tuning.
Ideal for custom serial queues or precise scheduling.
Requires manual dispatch back to main for UI updates.
async/await

Use actors and @MainActor to manage isolated state safely.
Better readability and testability for many async flows.
Decision guide
Need explicit queue control or integrate C APIs? Use GCD.
Need structured cancellation, simpler composition, and better readability? Use async/await.

screens.title: MainActor and safe UI updates
screens.subtitle: How to use @MainActor to simplify UI state handling

narration.text: MainActor is a global actor that ensures code annotated with @MainActor runs on the main thread. For view models and objects that manage UI state, marking the class or specific properties with @MainActor is a pragmatic choice. This guarantees that assignments to @Published properties are executed on the main actor and removed the need for explicit DispatchQueue. main. async calls throughout your code. For example, an ImageLoader or DataFetcher annotated with @MainActor can set isLoading, data, and errorMessage directly in async code without additional dispatch. One misconception is that @MainActor makes code synchronous; it does not. It schedules the work on the main actor, preserving responsiveness and correctness. Use @MainActor for UI-facing state, but keep heavy processing off the main actor. If you need to perform C P U-heavy work, run it in Task. detached or on a global queue, then send final results to an actor-protected property. This balance simplifies reasoning about shared state and lowers the risk of race conditions for UI variables. MainActor and safe UI updates means mark ui-facing state with @mainactor so updates are scheduled on the main thread and ui code stays safe and simple.. In practical terms, how to use @mainactor to simplify ui state handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: MainActor rule
keyIdea.text: Mark UI-facing state with @MainActor so updates are scheduled on the main thread and UI code stays safe and simple.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › MainActor
Why use MainActor
Marking a view model with @MainActor means all its methods and property access execute on the main actor, ensuring UI safety without boilerplate dispatching.
It reduces accidental UI updates from background threads and simplifies code that manipulates @Published properties.
Use MainActor for view models and small controllers; keep performance-sensitive work off the actor.
Example annotation
@MainActor
class DataFetcher: ObservableObject {
  @Published var data: String = ""
  func fetchData() async { ... }
}
Key Takeaway

Use @MainActor to keep UI state updates safe and free your code from repetitive main-queue dispatches.

screens.title: Common concurrency pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Race conditions, deadlocks, retain cycles, and cancellation strategies

narration.text: Concurrency introduces several classes of bugs you must learn to spot. Race conditions occur when multiple tasks access and modify the same mutable resource without coordination; the result depends on timing. Avoid this by isolating mutable state on a single queue or using actors to provide isolated access. Deadlocks happen when tasks wait on each other indefinitely, often due to circular resource acquisition — avoid nested locks or blocking waits across queues. Retain cycles can arise when closures capture self strongly inside an async callback; use [weak self] or mark the owner with @MainActor and prefer structured Task usage that reduces lifetime leaks. Cancellation is another design concern: long-running work should check for cancellation and stop early, saving resources when a view disappears. Swift's Task cancellation model and TaskGroup help here. Finally, a misconception: more threads equal more speed. In many cases, excessive concurrency hurts performance due to context switching. The practical pattern is to limit concurrency to what your device can handle and prefer high-level constructs like TaskGroup or actors for safety and clarity. Common concurrency pitfalls and how to avoid them means use actors or serial queues for shared mutable state, avoid blocking waits, capture self weakly, and design cancellable tasks.. In practical terms, race conditions, deadlocks, retain cycles, and cancellation strategies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use actors or serial queues for shared mutable state, avoid blocking waits, capture self weakly, and design cancellable tasks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Pitfalls & Safety
Common issues
  • Race conditions: avoid by isolating mutable state on one queue or using actors.
  • Deadlocks: avoid blocking waits and circular resource locks.
  • Retain cycles: use weak captures or structured tasks to prevent leaks.
  • Cancellation: design tasks to check cancellation and return early.
Quick remedies
Use @MainActor or a dedicated serial queue for shared state.
Prefer TaskGroup for related async jobs and use Task.cancel for cooperative cancellation.
Audit closure captures for retain cycles and use weak self inside long-lived closures.
Warning

Avoid moving heavy work onto the main actor; it defeats the purpose of concurrency and causes UI blocking.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to remember. First, concurrency prevents UI blocking by allowing long-running tasks to run without freezing the main thread. Second, Grand Central Dispatch provides dispatch queues — use DispatchQueue. main for UI updates and DispatchQueue. global with appropriate QoS for background tasks. Third, Swift's async/await offers structured concurrency with async functions, await, Task, TaskGroup, and actors like MainActor for safer state handling. Pay attention to common pitfalls: race conditions, deadlocks, retain cycles, and cancellation design. Use actors or serialized queues to protect shared mutable state, mark UI-facing classes with @MainActor to simplify updates, and design cancellable tasks for long operations. Together, GCD and async/await give you the tools to write responsive, maintainable, and safe code. Which of these core concepts will you apply first in your next app?

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you code

narration.text: Before you start implementing concurrency in your app, keep three practical reminders in mind. First, always protect UI updates by ensuring they run on the main thread — use DispatchQueue. main or annotate your view model with @MainActor. Second, favor structured concurrency when possible: async/await, Task, and TaskGroup make code easier to read and cancel. Third, guard shared mutable state: use actors or a dedicated serial queue and avoid blocking waits that can deadlock. These reminders will help you reduce bugs and deliver a smooth user experience. As a final check, ask yourself: does this task need to be cancellable, and who owns the resulting state? Answering that will guide whether you use GCD, async/await, or actors.
